title: PromQL: rate, sum by, histogram_quantile
summary: Series and labels, why counters need rate(), aggregating with sum by, and how histogram_quantile turns buckets into a percentile (and where it lies).

steps.title: Series, counters, rate
body: Prometheus (3.16 in the lab) stores **time series**: a metric name plus a set of labels, with a sample every scrape.
```text
http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="shop", http_route="/api/checkout", http_response_status_code="502"}  1843
Counters only go up (and reset to 0 when the process restarts), so their raw value means nothing; you want the **per-second rate**:
- `rate(x_total[5m])`: average per-second increase over the last 5 minutes, handling resets. Use a window of at least 4 scrape
intervals. For alerts and dashboards.
- `irate(x_total[5m])`: from the last two samples only. Spiky; for zoomed-in graphs, never for alerts.
- `increase(x_total[1h])`: rate × window, "how many in the last hour" (extrapolated, so not always a whole number).
Then aggregate across instances: `sum by (http_route) (rate(...[5m]))` keeps only the labels you name; `sum without (instance)`
drops the ones you name. Always `rate` first, then `sum`: summing raw counters from instances that restarted at different times
breaks reset detection.
In Prometheus 3 the name you query is the OTLP name translated: dots to underscores, plus the unit and `_total`
(`http.server.request.duration` → `http_server_request_duration_seconds`). Prometheus 3 can also keep UTF-8 names
(`{"http.server.request.duration"}`) when you ingest OTLP directly, so check which your setup does.

steps.prompt: Which query answers "requests per second per route, all instances together"?
steps.explain: rate per series first (each series handles its own resets), then add them up. The second needs a subquery and breaks when one instance restarts; the third sums lifetime totals.

steps.title: rate() by hand
prompt: Implement the core of `rate()` for one counter series: `double Rate(List<(double T, double V)> samples)` (seconds, value):
- the increase is the sum of the differences between consecutive samples, except when a value **drops** (a counter reset: the
process restarted), where the increase for that step is the new value itself;
- rate = increase / (last T - first T); 0 with fewer than two samples.
(Real Prometheus also extrapolates to the edges of the window; leave that out.)
starter: double Rate(List<(double T, double V)> samples)
solution: double Rate(List<(double T, double V)> samples)
hints: Loop over consecutive pairs; a negative difference means the counter started again from 0.

steps.title: Histograms and histogram_quantile
body: A histogram is exported as cumulative buckets: `_bucket{le="0.1"}` counts observations ≤ 0.1 s, `le="+Inf"` counts all of them
(= `_count`), and `_sum` is their total. A percentile over 5 minutes, per route:
```text
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, http_route) (rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="shop"}[5m])))
Keep `le` in the `by`: the function needs the buckets. It finds the bucket where the 95th percentile falls and **interpolates
linearly** inside it, so the answer can only be as good as the boundaries: with buckets at 75 and 100 ms, a real p95 of 92 ms or
of 76 ms can both come out near 99. That is the flat line at ~0.098 s below, recorded in the lab while the product page was slow; the
index went in at the marked time and p95 dropped to the next bucket down. Average latency = `rate(_sum[5m]) / rate(_count[5m])`.
You cannot average percentiles across instances (the mean of two p95s is not the p95); you can always add buckets. That is the reason
to export histograms rather than precomputed percentiles.

steps.title: histogram_quantile by hand
prompt: Implement Prometheus' algorithm: `double Quantile(double q, List<(double Le, double Count)> buckets)`. Buckets are cumulative,
sorted by `Le`, and the last has `Le = double.PositiveInfinity`.
1. total = the count of the last bucket; if 0, return `double.NaN`.
2. rank = q × total. Find the first bucket whose count ≥ rank.
3. If that is the `+Inf` bucket, return the `Le` of the bucket before it (the largest finite bound).
4. Otherwise interpolate: lower bound = the previous bucket's `Le` (0 for the first bucket), count below = the previous bucket's
count (0 for the first); result = lower + (upper - lower) × (rank - countBelow) / (count - countBelow).
starter: double Quantile(double q, List<(double Le, double Count)> buckets)
solution: double Quantile(double q, List<(double Le, double Count)> buckets)
template: Dojo.Eq("the slow product page: p95 lands in the 75-100 ms bucket", 0.0992, Math.Round(Quantile(0.95, dojoSlow), 4));
Dojo.Eq("after the index: first bucket, lower bound 0", 0.005, Math.Round(Quantile(0.95, dojoFast), 4));
Dojo.Eq("p99 beyond the last finite bucket returns that bound", 0.5, Quantile(0.99, dojoTail));
